conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS, which looks at mood and anxiety in the first postpartum months. It’s completely confidential; anything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise, and my only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past week—no right or wrong answers, just whatever is true for you. Ready to start?

Looking back over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, not very often. I used to laugh a lot more—my husband and I would joke around all the time—but lately it feels like I’m just too tired or worried. Maybe once or twice I’ve cracked a smile at something, but it’s like the joy is buried under a pile of diapers and “what-ifs.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Mostly no. I can still laugh a little—like maybe once or twice when my husband sent me a silly meme—but it feels forced and fades fast. The rest of the time I’m too anxious or just flat to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even a shower without interruption—but now it all feels like one more thing I have to do. I’ll think “maybe I’ll enjoy that,” but when the time comes I’m just too tired or worried and I don’t bother.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes—pretty much every day. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right, like I missed a cue or didn’t feed him well enough. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat on the couch crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom for wasting it. I know in my head it’s not logical, but the guilt just jumps out before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, that happens a lot. I’ll be sitting there with the baby sleeping soundly, and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet—so I have to check his breathing over and over. Or I’ll worry the formula isn’t the right brand, or that I didn’t sterilize the bottles long enough. Nothing’s actually wrong, but I can’t shake the feeling that something bad is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. It’s not every day, but maybe a couple of times this week I’ll get this sudden wave of dread—like my chest feels tight and I think something awful is about to happen, even though everything looks fine. I’ll pace the hallway checking the locks or stand over the crib watching him breathe until the feeling passes. It’s scary because it comes out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most of the time. Feeding, changing, laundry, trying to sleep, worrying if I’m doing any of it right…it feels like a constant avalanche. I manage to get the basics done, but by evening I’m exhausted and snapping at my partner over little things. I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this,” but it just feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I’ll lie down once the baby’s finally asleep, but then my head starts spinning—did I burp him long enough, is he gaining enough weight, am I already failing him? I can’t turn it off, so I’m tossing and turning for an hour or two, and when I do drift off I jerk awake sure I heard him cry. Some nights I only get three broken hours, and I dread the next day before it even starts.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a heavy blanket I can’t push off. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but it’s tangled up with this constant ache, like I’m already disappointing him. Sometimes the sadness just sits in my throat and I end up crying while I fold laundry or warm up a bottle.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes. I’ve cried three or four times since last week—sometimes it’s triggered by something small like dropping a spoon, other times it just bubbles up while I’m rocking the baby. I try to hide it so my older kid doesn’t see, but I end up sobbing into a burp cloth, feeling stupid for crying over “nothing.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be a good mom.

You've shared that the last seven days have felt heavy-laughter feels forced, activities you used to anticipate now seem like burdens, and waves of guilt and worry crash over you many times a day. You described checking your sleeping baby's breathing over and over, crying while folding laundry, and lying awake for hours thinking you've already failed as a mom. Yet you were clear that you want to feel like yourself again and be the mom you know you can be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports minimal, fleeting laughter that feels forced—matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports inability to anticipate enjoyment and avoids previously pleasurable activities, aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, daily self-blame with intense guilt over minor incidents, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries (checking breathing, formula brand, sterilization) that occur without real danger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden dread, chest tightness, and compulsive checking behaviors occurring several times this week, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant overwhelm, exhaustion, irritability, and inability to cope despite completing basics, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing worries, resulting in severely fragmented sleep (≈3 h/night), aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent daily sadness described as a 'heavy blanket' and 'constant ache,' indicating severe and frequent misery matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms frequent crying triggered by minor events and describes inability to control tears, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 25 exceeds the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Daily <sym>anhedonia</sym>, pervasive <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>tearfulness</sym>, and <sym>middle-of-the-night rumination</sym> align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Periparton Onset</med>. Frequent <sym>panic-like surges</sym> and repetitive checking behaviors suggest comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. Patient denies self-harm, so immediate emergency intervention is not indicated, yet functional impairment is high and symptoms are persistent. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> and evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>
3. Discuss medication options compatible with breastfeeding if applicable
4. Share the 24/7 national Maternal Mental Health Hotline (1-833-943-5746) for immediate support
5. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or postpartum doula-for night feeds and household tasks to protect your sleep
6. Practice brief self-care moments (five-minute shower, stroller walk, deep-breathing) and note them as small wins
7. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress after treatment begins
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, 1–2 weeks post-delivery

Presenting Concerns  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (“terrible mom” cognitions)  
- Recurrent, intrusive worries about infant safety; nocturnal checking behaviors  
- Episodic panic-like surges (tight chest, dread) without clear trigger  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulty linked to racing worries  
- Subjective sense of being “overwhelmed” by routine tasks; irritability toward partner  

Pattern  
Responses consistent across all days this week; symptoms wax and wane but present daily, causing functional impairment (e.g., avoiding outings, snapping at partner).

Risk Factors  
- Daily sadness, crying spells, loss of enjoyment (Q1,2,8,9)  
- Pathological guilt / inadequacy (Q3)  
- Anxiety & panic symptoms (Q4,5)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood (Q7)  
- Negatives: No self-harm ideation, no psychotic features, no substance misuse reported

Screening Impression  
High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; patient denies self-harm. Safety plan reviewed; routine follow-up and formal diagnostic evaluation recommended within 1 week (sooner if symptoms escalate).
